verses.text: In Iconium, they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed.
But the disbelieving  Jews stirred up and embittered the souls of the Gentiles against the brothers.
Therefore they stayed there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
But the multitude of the city was divided. Part sided with the Jews, and part with the apostles.
When some of both the Gentiles and the Jews, with their rulers, made a violent attempt to mistreat and stone them,
they became aware of it, and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region.
There they preached the Good News.
At Lystra a certain man sat, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked.
He was listening to Paul speaking, who, fastening eyes on him, and seeing that he had faith to be made whole,
said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” He leaped up and walked.
When the multitude saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voice, saying in the language of Lycaonia, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!”
They called Barnabas “Jupiter”, and Paul “Mercury”, because he was the chief speaker.
The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was in front of their city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have made a sacrifice along with the multitudes.
But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes, and sprang into the multitude, crying out,

“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them;
who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways.
Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you  rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.”
Even saying these things, they hardly stopped the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them.
But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.
But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city. On the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe.
When they had preached the Good News to that city, and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
confirming the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.
When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they had believed.
They passed through Pisidia, and came to Pamphylia.
When they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work which they had fulfilled.
When they had arrived, and had gathered the assembly together, they reported all the things that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations.
They stayed there with the disciples for a long time.

footnotes.content: Boldness opens doors—when Paul and Barnabas walked into that synagogue in Iconium, they didn't whisper or apologize. They spoke so that both Jews and Greeks believed. The Lord often honors the courage to speak plainly about His grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's always resistance to the gospel. The disbelieving ones stirred up the crowd, poisoning hearts against the brothers. Even when the Lord is moving, we shouldn't be surprised when some turn bitter—it's the pattern in a world bent away from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord testified to His word through the apostles' hands—signs and wonders confirmed what they preached. Notice how long they stayed: they didn't run when opposition came, but kept speaking boldly, letting His grace do the proving work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Division is the fruit of the gospel's presence. When the city split—some with the Jews, some with the apostles—it wasn't a failure. The Word had divided, yes, but it had also awakened choice in the hearts that heard it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Persecution often begins in whispers of intent before it breaks into violence. Gentiles and Jews, rulers and ordinary folk, conspired together to stone them. It's humbling to see how quickly the world can unite against the gospel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord gives wisdom to flee when the hour comes. Paul and Barnabas didn't wait to be martyred—not yet—but slipped away to Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding cities of Lycaonia. Survival was part of the mission, and they knew it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They kept preaching. After fleeing, after being hunted, the Good News was still their one task. That's faithfulness—not the absence of fear, but the refusal to let fear silence the message.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This man had been crippled from birth—lifelong helplessness. He sat listening to Paul speak. Sometimes the greatest miracle isn't in the restoration itself, but in the moment when a soul, bound for so long, opens itself to the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul saw what others didn't: the man had faith to be made whole. In that gaze, something holy happened—a recognition that the Lord was already working in this crippled stranger's heart before any command was spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Stand upright on your feet!" One sentence, spoken with authority. The man leaped—suddenly whole, suddenly walking. This is how the Lord works: a word that calls into being what was impossible before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crowd's first thought was gods, not grace. We're quick to deify the messenger, to explain the miraculous as divine visitation rather than trust the God we don't see. The apostles were about to face the hardest correction: clarifying who deserves worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury because Paul was the speaker. How easily we name what we see, assigning the familiar god-faces to unexpected servants. But names don't change the truth of who these men served.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest of Jupiter brought oxen and garlands, ready to sacrifice. What an image: the machinery of false worship springing into motion because one healing happened. The powers of this age move fast when threatened by true power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles tore their clothes—the ancient gesture of horror and grief. They sprang into the crowd, desperate to stop the sacrifice. Sometimes love for the Lord and love for the deceived demands we act with urgency and visible distress.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We also are men of like passions with you." Paul and Barnabas made themselves plain—no mystery, no pretense—so they could point to the living God. The gospel travels best on the road of radical honesty and radical humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord allowed nations to walk in their own ways, in darkness. How patient He is, how long He bears with us. Yet patience is never indifference—He was already stirring hearts through Paul and Barnabas to turn back to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every good gift—rain, seasons, food, joy—is His witness. The Lord hasn't left Himself without a testimony even in the ordinary mercies of life. Sometimes the grandest proclamation of His love comes not from doctrine, but from a harvest, a full belly, a glad heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crowd hardly stopped even as the apostles pled. How stubborn is the human heart toward truth! Even the plainest words from Paul and Barnabas barely held back the tide of misplaced worship. Sometimes we're deaf even when love shouts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The persecutors from Antioch and Iconium tracked Paul down and incited the crowd to stone him. He was left for dead, dragged outside the city like refuse. The gospel's cost was made visible—not in theory, but in broken bones and blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this: as the disciples stood around Paul, he rose up. Beaten, stone-marked, but alive—and he walked back into the city. Looking back from a longer road, I see his rising as a shadow of Resurrection, a glimpse of the power that defeats death itself. As of 2026-10, that same power still speaks to broken hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They didn't leave him behind—they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch the next day. After declaring the Good News in Derbe, they went back to the very cities that had persecuted them, to gather disciples. Faithfulness means you don't run, not even after you're nearly killed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They told the young disciples plainly: through many afflictions we must enter God's Kingdom. No soft gospel here—just honest truth. The apostles weren't painting a false hope; they were saying, "The cost is real, but it's worth the kingdom."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elders were appointed in every assembly, set apart through prayer and fasting. The apostles left behind not just converts, but leadership—structure rooted in prayer. This is how the Church endures: by giving the young body shepherds to tend it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia—these names meant little to most. But for those who followed the apostles' journeys, each place was a waypoint where the gospel had been proclaimed, seed scattered on ground now far behind them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They spoke the word in Perga, then journeyed onward to Attalia. The ministry was woven into travel itself—not confined to one place, but flowing along the roads they walked. Sometimes the Lord preaches through pilgrimage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sailed back to Antioch, from where they'd been sent out and committed to God's grace. The journey had come full circle—they were returning as witnesses of what the Lord had done. Coming home changed, forever marked by His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They gathered the assembly and reported all that God had done. The phrase "He had opened a door of faith to the nations" is simple, but it captures it: the Lord Himself was opening what human hands could never unlock. The Gospel was breaking beyond its boundaries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They stayed there with the disciples for a long time. After the urgency, the travel, the danger—there was rest. The Lord gives space for the community to gather close, to be taught, to grow. This too is part of the work: being present, tending what has begun.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
